notes.text: Let us not lose sight of the fact that all through the history of Israel until the coming of our Redeemer, the blessings of the Holy Priesthood were restricted. It was not given universally to the tribes, but of necessity there had to be some faithful men upon whom the Melchizedek Priesthood was conferred. All of the prophets held the Melchizedek Priesthood, but the Prophet Joseph Smith has informed us that in each case it was by special divine appointment. There was never a time in Israel when there was not a prophet with divine authority with power to confirm and perform other ordinances. . . . So other prophets like Isaiah, Jeremiah. Ezekiel, and Daniel were blessed with the Melchizedek Priesthood. They could officiate among the people. but there was no universal bestowal of authority among the tribes, from the time of the entrance of Israel into the promised land, until the coming of our Savior. When he came, the fulness of the gospel and of divine authority was restored. (Joseph Fielding Smith, Answers to Gospel Questions., 5 vols. (Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Company, 1979), 4:159-160.)

quotes.text: Joseph Smith was ordained before he came here, the same as Jeremiah was. Said the Lord unto him, "Before you were begotten I knew you," etc. So do I believe with regard to this people, so do I believe with regard to the apostles, the high priests, seventies and the elders of Israel bearing the Holy Priesthood, I believe they were ordained before they came here; and I believe the God of Israel has raised them up and has watched over them from their youth, has carried them through all the scenes of life both seen and unseen, and has prepared them as instruments in His hands to take this kingdom and bear it off. If this be so, what manner of men ought we to be? If anything under the heavens should humble men before the Lord and before one another, it should be the fact that we have been called of God.
quotes.speaker: Wilford Woodruff
quotes.attr: Wilford Woodruff, Journal of Discourses 21:317, October 10, 1880

quotes.text: The word of the Lord came also to Jeremiah the prophet saying that before he was born the Lord "sanctified (him) and ordained (him) a prophet unto the nations." (Jeremiah 1:5.) These and other similar scriptures make it plain that man existed in a spiritual condition before coming here to this earth and that in that pre-existence he had his free agency or right to choose. How could some of those spirits as seen by Abraham have become noble and great except by faithfulness to God's cause? How came God to choose Abraham or Jeremiah before they were born? If we had the complete answer to these questions, we would no doubt learn that they and others stood up valiantly with Michael and his angels when "there was war in heaven. . . . and Satan and his angels were cast out" of heaven for rebellion. (Rev. 12:7-12.)
quotes.speaker: Harold B. Lee
quotes.attr: Harold B. Lee, Decisions for Successful Living, p.163-164

quotes.text: This passage is one of the few clear revelations about foreordination in the scriptures. It tells of Jeremiah's being sanctified for special service and ordained to be a prophet in his premortal life-in the spirit world, for it happened before his body was even formed (Jer. 1:5 and fn.). Nevertheless, like Moses and Enoch before him, Jeremiah felt inadequate for his calling (Jer. 1:6). The Lord assured him he would be able to go where divinely sent and speak what he would be commanded to speak, but he must not be afraid. The Lord touched Jeremiah's mouth and assigned him six difficult tasks as a reformer (Jer. 1:6-10 and fn.).

notes.text: The charge "to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy" is also referred to at other times in Jeremiah's prophecies (see 12:17; 18:7). Jeremiah's mission was to all the nations and kingdoms, not just Judah. In carrying out his mission, he prophesied against all the surrounding nations as well as against Judah (see chapters 46-51 of Jeremiah and chapter 15 of this work). The charge "to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy" was a charge to testify against the evils of the day and to call the people to repentance; this Jeremiah did throughout his ministry. His mission was also "to build, and to plant." The captives who were taken into the land of the Chaldeans were to return and be built and planted (see 24:6). Those who were to be restored in the latter-days were likewise to be built and planted (see 31:28). Following the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, those who were allowed to remain in the land were promised that if they did remain they would be built up and not pulled down, they would be planted and not plucked out (see 42:10). However, they rejected this opportunity and went into Egypt, where they were pulled down and destroyed. Jeremiah's call might be compared to Joseph Smith's call to raise a voice of warning to all the inhabitants of the earth (see D&C 1). and to the angel Moroni's declaration to Joseph "that God had a work for me [Joseph] to do; and that my name should be had for good and evil among all nations, kindreds, and tongues, or that it should be both good and evil spoken of among all people" (Joseph Smith-History 1:33). (Monte S. Nyman, The Words of Jeremiah , p.18-19) 1:11-12. The meaning of the vision of the almond tree is uncertain. Because the almond tree is the first tree to blossom in the spring, some commentators emphasize that this is a watchful twig, the first to open its eyes. Others emphasize that the vision shows, not a flowering branch, but a rod which is to be used as a stick to beat with, or a rod of correction. Others emphasize a wordplay between the Hebrew words for "almond" and "watching," showing by association that Jehovah is watching over his word to bring it to pass. Until further knowledge of "the manner of prophesying among the Jews" is given (see 2

quotes.text: Nephi 25:1-2), the interpretation of the almond rod cannot be definitely ascertained. ).
